opus-5.5.text:
I don't really see them as opposing forces, though people often frame it that way. Scale buys you an enormous amount: coverage of the long tail, robustness, a kind of general visual common sense you can't hand-engineer. Early on, a lot of us were surprised by how far you could get just by throwing more noisy web data and more compute at the problem.

But once you're working at that scale, curation becomes a lever with huge returns. Data quality shows up directly in the outputs. If your dataset is full of watermarks, low-resolution images, bad crops, or captions that don't actually describe the image, the model learns all of that faithfully. So a lot of the practical gains we've seen recently come less from adding more data and more from being smarter about which data you keep, how you caption it, and how you balance it.

The way I think about it is roughly in stages. In pre-training you want breadth, so you're fairly permissive and filter out mostly the obvious garbage and anything harmful. Later in training you get much more selective: higher aesthetic quality, better text-image alignment, more careful captions. That later phase has an outsized effect on what users actually perceive as quality.

Curation also has a cost people underestimate. Every filter you apply carries assumptions. An aesthetic classifier encodes someone's taste, and aggressive filtering can quietly remove diversity, whether that's certain styles, cultures, or kinds of photography. So you have to be deliberate and measure what you're losing, not just what you're cleaning up.

Short answer: scale gets you capability, curation shapes how that capability shows up, and the interesting work right now is in getting the two to work together rather than picking one.

r001.rationale: The response treats scale and curation as complementary and says the work is to make them work together “rather than picking one,” so it does not predict that either approach will prove more successful.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think of those as less in tension than people usually frame them. The way it gets talked about is scale versus curation, like you have to pick a religion. But in practice, at least in the work I've been involved with, they've been complementary, and the interesting question is really about where in the pipeline each one does its work.

Scale is what gets you coverage. If you want a model that understands a very wide range of concepts, styles, compositions, lighting conditions, you just need to have seen a lot of the world, and there's no substitute for that. The early text-to-image results that surprised everyone were largely a story about data volume. You throw hundreds of millions of image-text pairs at a diffusion model and suddenly it knows what a "watercolor of a fox in a library" looks like, even though that exact thing was never in the training set.

But what we've found is that scale alone gives you a model that is broad but kind of mediocre at any given thing. It averages over everything it's seen. And a lot of what's on the internet is low quality: compressed, poorly composed, mislabeled, captions that have nothing to do with the image. So if your objective is, say, aesthetically pleasing outputs, or faithful prompt following, the raw distribution of the web is actually working against you.

That's where curation comes in, and I'd really split it into two things. One is filtering, which is removing stuff that's actively hurting you, and the other is what you might call shaping, which is deliberately overweighting the kind of data that reflects what you want the model to do. The second one turns out to matter a lot more than people expected. Things like recaptioning images with more descriptive, accurate text have had an outsized effect on controllability, and that's a curation move, not a scale move.

The way I'd summarize our current thinking is: use scale for pretraining, where the goal is to learn a rich representation of the visual world, and then get progressively more selective as you move toward the behavior you actually want. So it's not a tradeoff so much as a schedule. You're trading breadth for quality at different stages, and the mistake is trying to do both at the same stage.

The one place I'd push back on the pure scaling story is the cost side. Compute keeps getting cheaper, but good data doesn't, and we're already at the point where the quality of your data pipeline is a bigger differentiator between labs than parameter count. So if I had to bet on where the leverage is over the next couple of years, it's in understanding your data much better, not just in getting more of it.

r001.rationale: The response does not decline to predict which approach will be more successful. It favors improving data pipelines, saying that is where it would place its bet, while also describing scale and curation as complementary.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary. Scaling gives you broader coverage and more capacity, but it doesn’t remove the need to think carefully about what the model is learning from. If you scale a dataset with the same biases or quality issues, you can scale those problems too.

And curation isn’t necessarily about keeping only beautiful, polished images. You want diversity, you want unusual examples, and you want the relationship between an image and its caption to be useful. Filtering too aggressively can take away precisely the coverage you were hoping to get from scale.

So I’d frame it as: given a fixed compute budget, what data makes that training most valuable? Then you need to evaluate both the overall quality and the cases where the model struggles. More data can help, but understanding which data helps is a big part of the problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes scaling and curation as complementary but does not clearly decline to predict which approach will prove more successful.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re complementary. Scaling gives you broader coverage, but it also scales whatever problems are in the data—duplicates, poor captions, biases. So the question is less “scale or curate?” and more “what data makes additional scale useful?”

With images, curation is tricky because quality isn’t one-dimensional. A clean, aesthetically pleasing image might be useful for one task, while a blurry image of an unusual scene might be valuable for another. If you filter too aggressively, you can lose diversity and end up with a model that performs well on a narrow slice of the world.

I’d want to evaluate those choices together: as you increase the amount of data and compute, which kinds of filtering actually improve the capabilities you care about, and which just make the dataset look cleaner?

r001.rationale: The response does not predict which approach will prove more successful. It calls scaling and curation complementary, reframes the choice, and says their effects should be evaluated together.
